Menelaus Proof

GeometryTrianglesAlgebra
Game: Move the dots on a triangle's sides and watch the three side dots stay on one straight line.
How to play: Drag a dot with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Try Plain, Proof #1, Proof #2 and Proof #3, show the names, or start a fresh triangle.
Look for the math

Three dots, one on each side of a triangle, hardly look as if they must line up. Yet once they do, a simple product of three length ratios locks in place — and it stays locked however you pull the corners around. This applet draws the two proofs on the page plus a third picture of the same idea.

One line across three sides

Take F on AB, D on BC and E on CA. They may sit on the sides themselves or on the lines beyond them; a straight line cannot cut through all three sides inside the triangle, so at least one dot lies outside. The Menelaus theorem says the three dots are on one straight line exactly when

AF/BF · BD/CD · CE/AE = 1

With signed lengths the same statement reads AF/FB · BD/DC · CE/EA = −1, because reversing a segment changes its sign. The logic test checks both forms on the starting diagram, on fixed triangles and on hundreds of random ones: both hold every time, and moving any dot off the line breaks them. Its converse holds too — if the product is 1, the third dot must be where the line through the other two crosses the side.

Proof 1: one parallel line

Press Proof #1. Through A a line is drawn parallel to DE, and it meets line BC at P. The two pairs of similar triangles ABP and BDF, and ACP and CDE, give AF/BF = PD/BD and AE/CE = PD/CD. Dividing one by the other cancels PD and leaves the product equal to 1.

Proof 2: three perpendiculars

Press Proof #2. Drop a perpendicular from each corner onto the transversal, landing at Ha, Hb and Hc. Similar right triangles give AF/BF = AHa/BHb, BD/CD = BHb/CHc and CE/AE = CHc/AHa. Multiply them: the three heights cancel, leaving 1. The applet's third picture, Proof #3, takes a point K on the transversal, draws the perpendicular there, and shows the same heights as projections Ka, Kb and Kc.

Why dragging cannot break it

Each corner is free, but each side dot is glued to its own line. After a corner moves, the applet puts the dot on the far side back onto the new line and rebuilds the third dot as a line crossing, so the three dots are collinear again. Every reachable position has product 1 — that is the invariant the picture demonstrates. The sibling applets ask you to make a condition happen; this one begins with it already true and shows why. It is a demo: there is no winning or losing move. Compare Ceva's theorem, where the same product 1 means three cevians meet at a point rather than three dots lining up.

Try dragging F far past A, then press Proof #1 and watch P run along line BC while the product stays at 1. Press 1 to 4 on the keyboard to switch views.
